summary: Defines EAP-TLS, an EAP method that uses TLS for certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation. It builds on the EAP framework of RFC 3748. It replaces RFC 2716 and is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Both sides show an ID card to each other, and then they make a secret key. EAP-TLS lets computer and network prove who they are with certificates.

subtitle: How a device and a network prove who they are to each other with certificates, carried inside EAP.

tldr.problem: Networks that use EAP to let devices in need an authentication method where both sides prove their identity and end up with fresh keys. The EAP methods in RFC 3748 did not support mutual authentication.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-TLS runs a normal TLS handshake inside EAP packets, with a certificate on each side. It then derives keying material (the MSK and EMSK) from the TLS master secret and hands it to the lower layer.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2716 and is a Proposed Standard, and it has since been updated by RFC 8996, RFC 9190 and RFC 9965. Its requirements about which TLS versions and cipher suites to use should be read together with those updates.

today: RFC 5216 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2716. It is updated by RFC 8996, RFC 9190 and RFC 9965, so read those alongside it, especially for the TLS versions and cipher suites it requires.

sections.title: Why EAP Needs TLS
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP, RFC 3748) is a framework that lets many authentication methods be plugged into link layers such as PPP, IEEE 802.1X wired networks and IEEE 802.11 wireless networks. The methods defined in RFC 3748 did not support mutual authentication, but wireless LANs need a method that does, and that derives keys.

EAP-TLS fills this gap. It uses the cipher suite negotiation, mutual authentication and key management of TLS (version 1.1 in RFC 4346) and wraps them in EAP packets. It obsoletes RFC 2716 and remains backward compatible with it.

The RFC names four roles. The peer is the entity that responds (called the Supplicant in IEEE 802.1X). The authenticator starts the EAP exchange. The EAP server is the entity that actually terminates the method with the peer, and it may sit on a separate backend authentication server, in which case the authenticator just passes packets through.
sections.plainLanguage: A club needs a way for members and the door guard to check each other's ID. EAP-TLS is a ready-made ID check that both sides already know how to do.

sections.title: The EAP-TLS Conversation
sections.content:
After the usual EAP identity exchange, the EAP server sends an EAP-TLS/Start packet: an EAP-Request with the Start (S) bit set and no data. The peer answers with a TLS client_hello. The offered TLS version MUST be TLS v1.0 or later.

The server replies with a server_hello and, for a new session, a certificate chain, optionally a server_key_exchange, a certificate_request and server_hello_done. The server SHOULD ask the peer to authenticate, though that is not mandatory (the RFC mentions emergency services as a case where it may not be needed).

The peer then sends its certificate, client_key_exchange, certificate_verify, change_cipher_spec and finished. The server verifies the certificate and signature and answers with its own change_cipher_spec and finished. The peer sends an empty EAP-Response and the server finishes with EAP-Success.

Session resumption shortens this. If the server recognises the peer's sessionId, it sends only change_cipher_spec and finished after its server_hello, and the peer replies with the same two messages. This supports the fast reconnect of RFC 3748, and the RFC notes it works best when authentication is remoted to a shared backend server.

Termination is explicit. If the peer fails authentication, the server SHOULD send a TLS alert and then, after the peer's reply, an EAP-Failure. If the server fails authentication, the peer SHOULD delete the session from its cache, and the server MUST answer with EAP-Failure because server authentication failure is a terminal condition. A server that allows restarts SHOULD set a per-peer limit to resist denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: First the guard asks for your name. Then you and the guard swap ID cards and agree on a secret handshake. If either ID looks fake, the door stays shut and someone says why.

sections.title: Identity Privacy
sections.content:
By default the peer's username is visible in the EAP-Response/Identity and in its certificate. EAP-TLS implementations MAY support privacy: the peer sends an anonymous Network Access Identifier in the identity response, and sends its real certificate only after the TLS session is encrypted.

To do this, a privacy-configured peer MUST negotiate a cipher suite that provides confidentiality and MUST answer the first certificate_request with an empty certificate list. A privacy-supporting server MUST NOT treat that as fatal. It brings up the TLS session, sends a hello_request, and a second handshake follows in which the peer MUST provide at least one certificate. If it does not, the server MUST abort. Keying material is computed from the master_secret of the second handshake.

A peer configured for privacy usually cannot authenticate to a server that lacks privacy support, because such a server treats the refusal to send a certificate as an error. So peers SHOULD only be configured for privacy on networks known to support it.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of shouting your name at the door, you first whisper through a sealed tube, and only then show your ID card inside it so nobody in the hallway sees it.

sections.title: The EAP-TLS Packet
sections.content:
EAP-TLS Request and Response packets share one layout. They carry the standard EAP Code (1 for Request, 2 for Response), a one-octet Identifier, a two-octet Length, and a Type of 13 for EAP-TLS. Then come a Flags octet, an optional four-octet TLS Message Length, and the TLS data in TLS record format.

The flag bits are L (length included), M (more fragments) and S (EAP-TLS Start). Only the server's Start message uses S; the Response packet has no S bit. Reserved bits MUST be set to zero and ignored on reception.

The Identifier MUST change on each Request, and a Response MUST carry the Identifier of the Request it answers. Octets beyond the Length field are treated as data link padding and ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is an envelope with a small label on the front saying how long it is, whether it is the first of a set, and whether more envelopes follow.

sections.title: Fragmentation
sections.content:
A TLS record can be up to 16384 octets and a TLS certificate message may in principle be as long as 16 MB, while a RADIUS packet is limited to 4096 octets. A round of TLS messages can therefore be too big for one EAP packet, so an EAP-TLS implementation MUST provide its own fragmentation and reassembly.

Because EAP is a simple ACK-NAK protocol, this is simple. No fragment offset is needed, since the Identifier gives the sequence. The first fragment sets L and carries the TLS Message Length (the total size, to help buffer allocation), and every fragment except the last sets M. A receiver of a fragment with M set MUST reply with an empty EAP-TLS packet as an acknowledgement, and the sender MUST wait for it before sending the next fragment.

To guard against reassembly lockup and denial of service, an implementation may cap the size of one group of TLS messages. The RFC suggests 64 KB as a reasonable maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: If a parcel is too big for the mailbox, you send it in pieces and the other side says got it after every piece.

sections.title: Keys and Identities
sections.content:
EAP-TLS derives its exported keys from the TLS master secret through the TLS pseudo-random function, using the label client EAP encryption and the client and server random values. This gives the Master Session Key (MSK) and the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK), plus an initialization vector. The derivation is one-way, so the master secret cannot be recovered from them unless the PRF is broken, but if the master secret is compromised so are the MSK and EMSK.

The MSK is split into two 32-octet halves: the peer-to-authenticator key and the authenticator-to-peer key. The first is also known as the PMK in IEEE 802.11. How the keys are used is specific to the lower layer.

Identities come from the certificates. The Peer-Id and Server-Id are taken from the subjectAltName when present, otherwise from the subject. A host should have a dnsName, and a user an rfc822Name in NAI form. Since the identity in EAP-Response/Identity need not match the certificate, implementations SHOULD NOT require that they match, and a mismatched identity is unauthenticated and SHOULD NOT be used for access control or accounting.
sections.plainLanguage: Once you have both shown ID, you make a secret code only the two of you know. The code is built so that nobody can work backwards from it to your first secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists security claims in the EAP format: certificate-based authentication, cipher suite negotiation, mutual authentication, integrity and replay protection, key derivation, dictionary attack protection, fast reconnect and fragmentation, with no channel binding. Confidentiality is claimed only through the optional privacy feature. The claimed security proof assumes the peer and server key pairs are not shared, so a backend server supporting EAP-TLS SHOULD NOT use the same certificate with https.

Certificate handling. Servers SHOULD support RFC 3280 path validation. Because the peer may have no Internet access yet, the server SHOULD send its whole chain except the root. After the handshake, both sides MUST check that the certificate identity is authorized for EAP-TLS, and SHOULD check Extended Key Usage for server or client use. Implementations MUST support Certificate Revocation Lists and SHOULD support OCSP. A peer without connectivity may not be able to check revocation until after authentication, so peers and servers SHOULD implement Certificate Status Request, and peers MUST support checking revocation afterwards.

Packet modification. The Code, Identifier, Length, Type and Flags fields are not integrity protected. Extra data beyond Length could cause a buffer overrun in code that does not check, and changing Type could enable a downgrade attack toward another TLS-based EAP method or an inferior cipher suite.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID check is strong, but the label on the outside of the envelope is not sealed, so a sneaky person could scribble on it. Careful guards check that the label makes sense.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 1 for a Request, 2 for a Response.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Matches responses to requests; changes on each Request.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the EAP packet including Code, Identifier, Length, Type and Data.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: L, M and S bits, then reserved bits.

fields.name: TLS Message Length
fields.desc: Four octets in all, present only if L is set: the total length of the fragmented TLS message.

viz.caption: FLAG BITS IN THE FLAGS OCTET (RFC 5216, SECTION 3.1)

items.label: Length included
items.desc: A four-octet TLS Message Length field is present. MUST be set on the first fragment.

items.label: More fragments
items.desc: Set on all but the last fragment.

items.label: EAP-TLS start
items.desc: Set only in the Start message from server to peer.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: MUST be zero and ignored on reception.
